stem: How many diodes are used in a bridge rectifier?

options.content: Four
options.rationale: Correct: arranged in a diamond, two conducting in each half-cycle.

options.content: One
options.rationale: One diode gives half-wave rectification.

options.content: Two
options.rationale: Two diodes can give full-wave rectification only with a centre-tapped transformer, not a bridge.

options.content: Three
options.rationale: A bridge is symmetrical: four diodes.

explanation: A bridge rectifier has four diodes; two conduct during each half-cycle.

stem: A 50 Hz supply is full-wave rectified. How many peaks per second does the output voltage have?

options.rationale: Correct: both half-cycles give a positive hump.
That is for half-wave rectification.
Rectification never reduces the number of humps below the supply frequency.
Each cycle has two halves, giving two humps, not four.

explanation: Two humps per cycle × 50 cycles per second = 100 per second.

stem: Where is the smoothing capacitor connected in a rectifier circuit?

options.content: In series with the load resistor
options.rationale: In series it would block the direct current.

options.content: In series with the a.c. supply, before the diodes
options.rationale: It would then pass a.c. and not smooth the output.

options.content: Across one of the diodes in the bridge
options.rationale: That would short out the diode for a.c. and disturb rectification.

options.content: In parallel with the load resistor
options.rationale: Correct: it supplies the load between peaks.

explanation: The capacitor is in parallel with the load, charging at each peak and discharging through the load between peaks.

stem: A smoothed rectifier supplies a load. Which change would reduce the ripple?

options.content: Reducing the smoothing capacitance
options.rationale: A smaller C gives a smaller RC and more ripple.

options.content: Changing from full-wave to half-wave rectification
options.rationale: Half-wave doubles the time between peaks, increasing the ripple.

options.content: Connecting a second load in parallel with the first
options.rationale: This lowers the total load resistance, so RC falls and ripple grows.

options.content: Increasing the load resistance
options.rationale: Correct: larger RC, so less discharge between peaks.

explanation: Ripple is small when RC ≫ time between peaks; a larger R (smaller load current) increases RC.
hints: Compare RC with the time between peaks.

stem: In a smoothed half-wave rectifier, what is happening to the diode while the capacitor is supplying the load between peaks?

options.content: It is forward-biased and the capacitor discharges back through it.
options.rationale: A diode does not conduct in the reverse direction.

options.content: It is reverse-biased, because the capacitor p.d. is higher than the supply p.d.
options.rationale: Correct: no current flows from the supply until the next peak.

options.content: It is conducting and recharging the capacitor continuously.
options.rationale: Recharging happens only for a short time near each peak.

options.content: It is short-circuited by the capacitor.
options.rationale: The capacitor is across the load, not across the diode.

explanation: After the peak the supply falls below the capacitor p.d., so the diode is reverse-biased until the next rising hump exceeds it.
hints: Compare the supply p.d. with the capacitor p.d. after the peak.

stem: A $9.0\ \text{V}$ r.m.s. supply is full-wave rectified with ideal diodes. What is the peak output voltage?

options.rationale: This divides by √2: the peak is larger than the r.m.s. value.
Full-wave rectification does not double the peak.
Correct: √2 × 9.0.
9.0 V is the r.m.s. value of the supply, not its peak.

stem: A $470\ \mu\text{F}$ smoothing capacitor is connected across a $680\ \Omega$ load. Calculate the time constant, in s, to three significant figures.
explanation: $RC = 680 \times 470 \times 10^{-6} = 0.320\ \text{s}$, much longer than the $10\ \text{ms}$ between peaks of a full-wave rectified 50 Hz supply.
workedSolution: 1. $RC = 680 \times 470 \times 10^{-6} = 0.320\ \text{s}$, much longer than the $10\ \text{ms}$ between peaks of a full-wave rectified 50 Hz supply.

stem: A $15\ \text{V}$ r.m.s. supply feeds a bridge rectifier made of silicon diodes, each with a forward voltage of $0.70\ \text{V}$. Calculate the peak voltage across the load, in V, to three significant figures.
explanation: $\sqrt{2} \times 15 = 21.2\ \text{V}$; two diodes conduct at a time, so subtract $1.40\ \text{V}$: $19.8\ \text{V}$.
workedSolution: 1. $\sqrt{2} \times 15 = 21.2\ \text{V}$; two diodes conduct at a time, so subtract $1.40\ \text{V}$: $19.8\ \text{V}$.
hints: How many diodes are in the current path at any instant?

stem: A full-wave rectified $50\ \text{Hz}$ supply has a peak of $12.0\ \text{V}$. It is smoothed by a $1000\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor and feeds a $330\ \Omega$ load. Using $\Delta V = V_0\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)$, where $t$ is the time between peaks, estimate the ripple voltage, in V, to two significant figures.
explanation:
1. $RC = 330 \times 1000 \times 10^{-6} = 0.330\ \text{s}$.
2. Full-wave: $t = \dfrac{1}{2 \times 50} = 0.010\ \text{s}$.
3. $\Delta V = 12.0\left(1 - e^{-0.010/0.330}\right) = 0.36\ \text{V}$. Using $t = 0.020\ \text{s}$ (half-wave) would double it.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $RC = 330 \times 1000 \times 10^{-6} = 0.330\ \text{s}$.
2. Full-wave: $t = \dfrac{1}{2 \times 50} = 0.010\ \text{s}$.
3. $\Delta V = 12.0\left(1 - e^{-0.010/0.330}\right) = 0.36\ \text{V}$. Using $t = 0.020\ \text{s}$ (half-wave) would double it.
hints: Time between peaks is half the period for full-wave.

stem: A designer needs the ripple on a full-wave rectified $50\ \text{Hz}$ supply (peak $18\ \text{V}$) feeding a $250\ \Omega$ load to be no more than $0.50\ \text{V}$. Using $\Delta V \approx \dfrac{V_0t}{RC}$ with $t$ the time between peaks, calculate the minimum smoothing capacitance, in µF, to two significant figures.
explanation:
1. $C = \dfrac{V_0t}{R\,\Delta V} = \dfrac{18 \times 0.010}{250 \times 0.50}$.
2. $C = 1.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{F} = 1400\ \mu\text{F}$; a standard $1500\ \mu\text{F}$ or larger capacitor would be chosen. (The exponential form gives 1400 µF.)
workedSolution:
1. 1. $C = \dfrac{V_0t}{R\,\Delta V} = \dfrac{18 \times 0.010}{250 \times 0.50}$.
2. $C = 1.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{F} = 1400\ \mu\text{F}$; a standard $1500\ \mu\text{F}$ or larger capacitor would be chosen. (The exponential form gives 1400 µF.)
hints: t = 10 ms for full-wave at 50 Hz.

stem: A smoothed full-wave supply holds a $120\ \Omega$ load at about $12.0\ \text{V}$ using a $2700\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor (50 Hz mains). Treating the load current as constant between peaks, calculate the charge the capacitor loses between peaks and hence the ripple, in V, to two significant figures.
explanation: $I \approx \dfrac{12.0}{120} = 0.100\ \text{A}$; $\Delta Q = It = 0.100 \times 0.010 = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{C}$; $\Delta V = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{C} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2700 \times 10^{-6}} = NaN\ \text{V}$.

stem: On an oscilloscope set to $0.20\ \text{V div}^{-1}$ (with the d.c. level removed), the ripple appears $1.7 \pm 0.2$ divisions high. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the ripple, and suggest whether a more sensitive Y-gain should be used.
explanation: $\dfrac{0.2}{1.7} \times 100 = 12\%$. This is large: using $0.10\ \text{V div}^{-1}$ would double the trace height (3.4 divisions) and halve the percentage uncertainty.
workedSolution: 1. $\dfrac{0.2}{1.7} \times 100 = 12\%$. This is large: using $0.10\ \text{V div}^{-1}$ would double the trace height (3.4 divisions) and halve the percentage uncertainty.

stem: In a bridge rectifier, the current through the load is in the same direction during both halves of each a.c. cycle.
explanation: True. Different pairs of diodes conduct in each half-cycle, but both pairs send current through the load in the same direction.

stem: Match each output (described in words) with the circuit that produces it.

left.content: Positive half-sine humps separated by gaps of zero p.d.
Positive half-sine humps with no gaps
Nearly steady p.d. with a small sawtooth ripple
Sine wave alternating above and below zero

right.content: Bridge rectifier with a capacitor across the load
Supply connected directly to the load
One diode in series with the load

explanation: Diodes remove or reverse the negative halves; the capacitor fills the gaps between peaks.

stem: What name is given to converting alternating current into current in one direction only?
explanation: **Rectification**, done with diodes.

stem: Describe how a bridge of four diodes produces full-wave rectification. You may label the diodes D1 to D4.

points.description: Supply connected across one diagonal of the bridge; load across the other.
In one half-cycle, two diodes on opposite sides (e.g. D1 and D3) are forward-biased and conduct; the other two are reverse-biased.
In the next half-cycle, the other pair (D2 and D4) conducts.
Both pairs direct current through the load in the same direction, so the load p.d. has the same polarity throughout (humps with no gaps).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The a.c. supply is connected across one diagonal of the diamond of diodes and the load across the other. In the first half-cycle D1 and D3 are forward-biased and conduct, while D2 and D4 are reverse-biased. In the second half-cycle the supply reverses, so D2 and D4 conduct instead. Both routes take the current through the load in the same direction, so the output is a series of positive half-sine humps with no gaps.

explanation: Two diodes conduct per half-cycle; load current always in one direction.
hints: Which diodes conduct when the top supply terminal is positive?

stem: Describe the graph of output voltage against time for a full-wave rectifier with a smoothing capacitor, as you would sketch it, and explain its shape.

points.description: Voltage stays close to the peak value V₀ (never falls to zero).
Between peaks: a gentle (exponential) fall as the capacitor discharges through the load.
Near each peak (every half-cycle): a short, steep rise as the next hump recharges the capacitor, giving a small sawtooth ripple.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The output stays close to the peak voltage. After each peak it falls slowly and almost linearly (part of an exponential decay) as the capacitor discharges through the load; then, as the next rectified hump rises above the capacitor p.d., it rises steeply back to the peak. This gives a small sawtooth ripple with two cycles per supply cycle.

explanation: Slow discharge, fast recharge: sawtooth ripple near V₀.
hints: What happens between peaks, and what happens at each peak?

stem: State two advantages of full-wave rectification over half-wave rectification.

points.description: Both halves of each cycle are used, so more power is delivered (higher mean output) / energy is not wasted.
Twice as many peaks, so the time between peaks is halved and the ripple after smoothing is smaller (smaller capacitor needed).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Full-wave rectification uses both halves of every cycle, so the mean output and power delivered are greater; and because there are twice as many peaks, the capacitor discharges for only half as long between them, giving less ripple for the same capacitor.

explanation: More power; less ripple.

stem: A charger uses a transformer that gives $7.5\ \text{V}$ r.m.s. at $50\ \text{Hz}$, a bridge of silicon diodes (forward voltage $0.70\ \text{V}$ each), a $3300\ \mu\text{F}$ smoothing capacitor and a load that behaves as a $50\ \Omega$ resistor.

parts.stem: Calculate the peak voltage across the load, in V, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (b)

parts.label: (d)

parts.stem: If one diode of the bridge failed open-circuit, the circuit would act as a half-wave rectifier with only one diode drop. Estimate the new ripple, in V, to two significant figures.
parts.explanation: Now $t = 20\ \text{ms}$ and $V_0 \approx 9.91\ \text{V}$: $\Delta V = 9.91\left(1 - e^{-0.020/0.165}\right) = 1.1\ \text{V}$, about twice as large.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why the ripple increases when the phone draws more current.

points.description: A larger current means a smaller effective load resistance R.
So RC is smaller and the capacitor discharges more between peaks: larger ripple.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Drawing more current is equivalent to a smaller load resistance, so the time constant RC falls and the capacitor loses more of its charge between peaks, increasing the ripple.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Suggest two ways of making the output steadier.

points.description: Use a larger smoothing capacitance (larger RC).
Add a voltage regulator (e.g. Zener diode or regulator IC) after the capacitor / add a second filter stage.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Use a larger capacitor so that RC is longer, and follow it with a voltage regulator that holds the output constant despite the remaining ripple.

explanation: Peak = √2 × V_rms − diode drops; ripple ≈ V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)), t = time between peaks.

points.description: ΔV is approximately inversely proportional to C (ΔV × C roughly constant, about V₀t/R = 500 V µF).
Shown by calculating ΔV × C for 330, 680 and 1500 µF: nearly equal values.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: For the larger capacitors ΔV × C is nearly constant (about 460-490 V µF), so ΔV is approximately inversely proportional to C, as expected from ΔV ≈ V₀t/(RC).

points.description: RC = 0.030 s is not much larger than the 10 ms between peaks.
So the discharge is not approximately linear: the exponential curve flattens and ΔV is less than V₀t/(RC).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: With 150 µF, RC = 0.030 s, only three times the time between peaks, so the capacitor's exponential discharge cannot be treated as linear; the ripple is noticeably less than V₀t/(RC).

parts.stem: State the graph you would plot to test ΔV ∝ 1/C and what it would show if the relationship held.

points.description: A straight line through the origin (gradient V₀t/R).
